name: Le 19, Crac
funding: French state (DRAC Bourgogne-Franche-Comté), Région Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, City of Montbéliard and Pays de Montbéliard Agglomération.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: Names its four public funders in its About text.
affiliations_note: Member of d.c.a., Seize Mille, TRAC, Bla!, MÔM'ART and Une ouverture pour l'art, and the local relay for the Nouveaux Commanditaires.

overview: Regional centre for contemporary art at 19 avenue des Alliés, in the town centre of Montbéliard in front of the railway station (le19crac.com; DCA).

Founded in 1993 and opened in 1995. Since 2018 it holds the national label CACIN (Centre d'Art Contemporain d'Intérêt National) and belongs to the DCA network and the regional networks Seize Mille and TRAC (le19crac.com).
Building: a 1920s warehouse, formerly the first office of the Peugeot car company, with an industrial aesthetic (le19crac.com).

On site: a 550 m² exhibition space showing three to four exhibitions a year, plus off-site projects with partners. It supports artists financially and logistically, invites external curators and involves non-professionals (le19crac.com).
Director: Adeline Lépine-Delaborde (DCA member page).
Visiting: open Tuesday to Saturday 2 pm to 6 pm and Sunday 3 pm to 6 pm. Free entry (le19crac.com).
details.funding_verdict: Le 19, Crac: public: the State (DRAC Bourgogne-Franche-Comté), Région Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, the City of Montbéliard and the Pays de Montbéliard Agglomération
funding: The centre names its four public funders: the French government, the Burgundy-Franche-Comté Region, the City of Montbéliard and the Pays de Montbéliard Agglomération (le19crac.com).
The DCA member page names the State funder as the DRAC Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, the regional cultural affairs office (DCA).
details.bottom_line: The money behind Le 19 is public: the French State through the DRAC, the Bourgogne-Franche-Comté Region, the City of Montbéliard and the Pays de Montbéliard Agglomération, all named by the centre itself. Entry is free.

name: MAMAC
funding: One of 11 museums run by the City of Nice (museum website).
watch: A city museum of modern and contemporary art, closed since 7 January 2024 for renovation; the first architect's contract was ended and a new consultation launched in early 2025, with a reopening target of 2029. Céline Kopp became director on 1 January 2026.

overview: The MAMAC is the Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art of Nice, at Place Yves Klein, and is one of 11 museums run by the City of Nice (museum website).
It opened in 1990 and concentrates on post-war to present-day art, mainly European and American (Nice Premium, 25 September 2025).
What is there: the museum highlights Nouveau réalisme, Yves Klein and Niki de Saint Phalle and site-specific works (museum website). The pages read give no object count.
Archive: the pages read do not mention a library or archive. The museum closed on 7 January 2024 and shows its collection outside its walls (#MAMACnextdoor, loans and online).
details.funding_verdict: MAMAC: municipal funding, amounts not stated
funding: City of Nice: operator of the museum (museum website). The pages read give no budget, no renovation cost and no outside funders (Nice Premium, 2025).
No reporting found of sponsors.

red_flags.heading: Renovation project reset
points: Nice Premium reported that work began in 2024 with diagnostics and the securing of works, then the contract with the selected architect was ended because the project was too far from the city's expectations; a new architect consultation was launched at the start of 2025 and the reopening deadline remains 2029. The page records no named official.

red_flags.heading: Director succession
points: Hélène Guenin left after nine years; Johanne Lindskog, director of the Nice Fine Arts Museum, was interim from February 2025; Céline Kopp took over on 1 January 2026 (Nice Premium, 25 September 2025).

wider_context: Nice Premium reported on 30 November 2025 that about a dozen employees of the Magasin in Grenoble, which Céline Kopp has directed since 2022, described to media successive sick leaves, dismissals and labour court cases, that eight of eleven employees struck on 19 November 2025 for two hours, and that unions demanded mediation and an organisational audit. The article carries no reply from Kopp, the City or the Magasin.
details.bottom_line: The City of Nice runs and pays for it; the building has been closed since January 2024 and the first renovation architect was dropped. The new director comes from the Magasin in Grenoble, where staff complaints are reported below.

name: Musée d'arts de Nantes
funding: The six-year renovation and extension by Stanton Williams, reopened on 23 June 2017, cost 48.8 million euros according to The Spaces; the pages read do not name its funders.
watch: A fine arts museum founded in 1800, in a nineteenth-century palace and a seventeenth-century chapel, with a 4,000 square metre Cube for contemporary art added in 2017. The only cost figure is 48.8 million euros for the 2017 works.

overview: The Musée d'arts de Nantes is at 10 rue Georges Clemenceau, in a nineteenth-century palace with a seventeenth-century oratory chapel, and was formerly the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Nantes (The Spaces; Museofile record).
It was created in 1800 by a consular order, bought the Cacault collection in 1810 and opened a new building in 1900; it has been a musée de France since 5 January 2002 (Museofile record).

What is there: holdings of modern and contemporary art, fine arts (drawing, print and poster, painting, sculpture) and photography, with Italian painting from the thirteenth to eighteenth centuries, nineteenth-century French and Flemish painting and international contemporary art; The Spaces says nine centuries of works across 17,000 square metres. The pages read give no object count.
Archive: The Spaces says the site includes an archive; the Museofile record names no library or archive.
details.funding_verdict: Musée d'arts de Nantes: municipal museum, renovation cost 48.8 million euros reported, funders not named
funding: Renovation and extension over six years to 2017: 48.8 million euros (The Spaces, 22 June 2017); the article quotes Jean-Louis Jossic of the City of Nantes and does not name the funders.
No reporting found of annual funding, State or Region grants, or private patrons.
details.bottom_line: A municipal museum whose 2017 renovation is given at 48.8 million euros; who paid was not found. Nothing contested was found.

name: Villa Arson
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
highlight: Michel Marot designed the Villa Arson buildings, which make wide use of courtyards, terraces and gardens.

overview: National higher art school and contemporary art centre on a hill in the Saint Barthélemy neighbourhood of northern Nice, overlooking the city and the coast (Wikipedia).
The site has the school, the art centre, residencies, a publishing shop, a library and Radio Arson (Villa Arson website).

The estate was an 18th-century villa bought in 1812 by Pierre-Joseph Arson, later a hotel and then the Clinique de Cyrnos. In 1964 the city of Nice ceded it to the State for an art school that André Malraux wanted (French Wikipedia).
The new school buildings were designed by Michel Marot and inaugurated in 1972 (French Wikipedia).

In 2002 the Ministry of Culture designated it a grand établissement for contemporary art (Wikipedia), and in 2003 it became an établissement public administratif under the Ministry of Culture (French Wikipedia). Since 2020 it has been a component of the Université Côte d'Azur (French Wikipedia).

Directors: Sylvain Lizon from 2019 to 2025. Ulrika Byttner, formerly head of the École supérieure d'art et de design Le Havre-Rouen, named by Minister of Culture Rachida Dati after the board's opinion (Ministry of Culture press release, 19 January 2026).

Visiting: open to the public every afternoon from 14:00 to 18:00, until 19:00 in July and August. Exhibitions from 12 November 2026 to 4 April 2027 include a show on Édouard Glissant and one on Serge Hélénon (Villa Arson website).
details.funding_verdict: Villa Arson: public establishment under the French Ministry of Culture
funding: It is an établissement public administratif under the Ministry of Culture (French Wikipedia). Minister of Culture Rachida Dati named Ulrika Byttner director after the board's opinion (Ministry of Culture press release, 19 January 2026).

The Francis Bacon MB Art Foundation entered a partnership with Villa Arson in 2017 and awards a €10,000 "Villa Arson Artist Support Scholarship" every two years to a Villa Arson graduate with a DNSEP master's degree in painting or drawing (MB Art Foundation).
details.bottom_line: Villa Arson is a national school and art centre run as a public establishment under the French Ministry of Culture. The one private funding line documented is a €10,000 scholarship every two years from the Francis Bacon MB Art Foundation.

name: Altes Museum
funding: The Altes Museum is one of the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin. The pages read did not state who funds it or give amounts.
watch: Karl Friedrich Schinkel's building of 1823 to 1830 on the Lustgarten shows the Antikensammlung and part of the Münzkabinett. The collection grew from the art holdings of the Brandenburg electors and Prussian kings (museum website).
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: The pages read gave no accounts for the museum itself.

overview: The Altes Museum is a museum of classical antiquity in Berlin, housed in a building by Karl Friedrich Schinkel built from 1823 to 1830, with 18 Ionic columns and a rotunda that refers to the Pantheon (museum website).
The inscription above the columns says Friedrich Wilhelm III founded the museum in 1828; the museum's collection page gives 1830 as its opening (museum website).

What is there: the Antikensammlung shows the art and culture of Greeks, Etruscans and Romans, with vases, inscriptions, architectural elements, sculptures, bronzes and terracottas, jewellery, glass and carved ivory from the Aegean Bronze Age to the late Roman period, plus finds from Etruria, Cyprus and the northern Black Sea region. The pages read gave no object count (museum website).

The collection grew from the art collections of the electors of Brandenburg and the Prussian kings; castle records of 1648 list antiquities and the Thesaurus Brandenburgicus of 1701 documented many works (museum website).
The Münzkabinett adds ancient coins and related objects to the display (museum website).
Archive: the collection page links to acquisition and accession logs and a bibliography of the collection's publications; it does not describe their contents (museum website).
details.funding_verdict: Altes Museum: public, part of the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin; funding not stated on the pages read
funding: No reporting found of the museum's own budget on the pages read.
The Staatliche Museen zu Berlin run the museum; the pages read did not name its funders or amounts.

red_flags.heading: War losses and returns
points: During the Second World War objects were moved to bunkers and art objects in Berlin were seized by the Red Army; in 1958 the Soviet Union returned 'one-and-a-half million works of art' to the GDR (museum website, Antikensammlung page).

details.bottom_line: The pages read name no funder or sum for the Altes Museum, so who pays cannot be followed from them. What is on record is the collection's history of wartime seizure and partial return.

name: Bayerische Staatsoper
funding: Carried by the Free State of Bavaria, which the German Music Information Centre names as its 'Träger' under public sponsorship. The pages read did not state amounts or name corporate sponsors.
watch: Bavaria's state opera in the Nationaltheater in Munich (2,101 seats), led by Staatsintendant Serge Dorny with Vladimir Jurowski as music director. It ended Anna Netrebko's engagement in March 2022 over her closeness to Vladimir Putin and in March 2026 announced her return for a recital on 23 July 2027.

overview: The Bayerische Staatsoper is the state opera of Bavaria, playing in the Nationaltheater at Max-Joseph-Platz 2 in Munich (German Music Information Centre, miz.org).
The pages read did not give a founding date.

What is there: the opera company with the Bayerisches Staatsorchester, the chorus and the ballet under Laurent Hilaire; the main hall has 2,101 seats; Serge Dorny is Staatsintendant, Patrick Wasserbauer managing director and Vladimir Jurowski general music director, with Petr Popelka named from the 2029/30 season (miz.org, entry changed 16 June 2026).
details.funding_verdict: Bayerische Staatsoper: public, Free State of Bavaria
funding: Free State of Bavaria: 'Träger: Freistaat Bayern', listed under public sponsorship (miz.org). The pages read did not state amounts.
No reporting found of named corporate sponsors on the pages read.

red_flags.heading: Russia's war and the house's artists
points: The Staatsoper cancelled Anna Netrebko's engagement because of her closeness to Vladimir Putin; in the same days the city of Munich ended its work with Valery Gergiev as chief conductor of the Munich Philharmonic 'mit sofortiger Wirkung', a separate, city-run orchestra (Euronews, 1 March 2022).
Netrebko wrote that she is 'keine politische Person' and that it was not the right time for her to perform (Euronews, 1 March 2022).

OperaWire reported on 15 March 2026 that Netrebko returns on 23 July 2027 for a recital. Dorny said the house and Jurowski 'have clearly sided with Ukraine. This position is non-negotiable', that Netrebko no longer performs in Russia and has distanced herself from the war, and that 'Anna Netrebko will be invited to perform in opera productions in the future' (OperaWire, 15 March 2026).

not_related: The Munich Philharmonic, whose chief conductor Valery Gergiev the city of Munich dismissed in 2022, is a city orchestra and not part of the Bayerische Staatsoper (Euronews, 1 March 2022).
details.bottom_line: Bavaria pays; no figure and no sponsor list could be read. The contested decisions on the pages read are about artists close to the Russian state, dropped in 2022 and, in Netrebko's case, invited back for 2027.

name: Brücke-Museum
funding: The collection began as a gift to the State of Berlin by Karl Schmidt-Rottluff. taz reported on 5 March 2021 that the Berlin Senate had confirmed funding for the museum's plan to decolonise its work. The pages read did not state budget figures.
watch: The museum opened on 15 September 1967. Schmidt-Rottluff's estate holds about 100 objects from colonial contexts, which the museum has been reappraising and digitising since January 2021.
records_note: The pages read gave no accounts.

overview: The Brücke-Museum is a museum of the Brücke expressionists at Bussardsteig 9 in Dahlem, Berlin (museum website).
It opened on 15 September 1967; Karl Schmidt-Rottluff initiated its establishment in 1964 and donated to the State of Berlin, which laid the foundation for the collection (museum website).

What is there: works of the Brücke artists; the pages read gave no object count. Schmidt-Rottluff's estate also contains around 100 objects from colonial contexts, among them drums, sculptures and combs, from about 20 identified regions of origin (museum website; taz, 5 March 2021).
Archive: the pages read did not describe an archive or library.
details.funding_verdict: Brücke-Museum: public, funded through the State of Berlin; amounts not stated on the pages read
funding: Land Berlin: the museum's founding gift went to the State of Berlin (museum website); taz reported on 5 March 2021 that the Berlin Senate had confirmed funding for the plan to decolonise the museum.
No reporting found of annual grant figures or private sponsors on the pages read.

red_flags.heading: Colonial links of Brücke artists and collections
points: Since January 2021 the museum has worked on the critical reappraisal and digitisation of the roughly 100 colonial-context objects in Schmidt-Rottluff's estate, with experts from the regions of origin and decolonial activists, and has put images and key data on Wikimedia Commons (museum website).

taz reported on 5 March 2021 that the origin of many of these objects is largely unknown and that the museum planned an expert network on provenance, contact with a Cameroonian-German research project, and invitations to contemporary artists.
Lisa Marei Schmidt, then director, told taz that colonialism had been 'vollkommen vernachlässigt' (entirely neglected) in expressionism research (taz, 5 March 2021).

Curators Dorthe Aagesen and Beatrice von Bormann, quoted by taz, describe some artists' depictions of objects as having a 'karikaturistischen oder rassischen Beigeschmack'. No restitution claim is mentioned on the pages read.

details.bottom_line: A small public museum whose money comes through the State of Berlin; the pages read give no sums. What is contested is the colonial provenance of about 100 objects in Schmidt-Rottluff's estate and the expressionists' use of colonial imagery.

name: daadgalerie
funding: The Federal Foreign Office and the State of Berlin fund the Berliner Künstlerprogramm, which shows work at the daadgalerie.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
highlight: Works by current and former fellows of the Berliner Künstlerprogramm are presented at the daadgalerie in Kreuzberg.

overview: Exhibition space of the Berliner Künstlerprogramm (BKP) of the DAAD, the German Academic Exchange Service, a residency programme for international artists and cultural workers. Projects from the programme are shown in the daadgalerie and at other venues in Berlin, across Germany and abroad (stated by the programme).

The programme began in 1963 as a Ford Foundation initiative. The DAAD took it over in 1965 and renamed it the Artists-in-Berlin Program (Wikipedia). The gallery opened in 1978 in Henny Porten's former villa on Kurfürstenstraße in West Berlin and moved to Zimmerstraße near Checkpoint Charlie in 2005 (Wikipedia).

In January 2017 the gallery moved to Oranienstraße 161 in Kreuzberg, a former shoe department store built in 1910/12 by the architect Oskar Kaufmann. It has about 500 square metres over two floors: a 250 m² ground-floor gallery and a first-floor studio for about 100 visitors (taz, Linda Gerner, 17 January 2017).

The programme says it leaves Oranienstraße 161 by 30 September 2026. From 3 October its new season runs at the Grüner Salon of the Volksbühne, Rosa-Luxemburg-Platz, 10178 Berlin, and at other Berlin venues.
The programme shows exhibitions, readings, concerts, film screenings and performances by current and former guests of the programme.
Visiting: the Grüner Salon is currently not wheelchair accessible, for structural reasons (stated by the programme). Events there have been listed with free admission.
details.funding_verdict: daadgalerie: public programme: run by the DAAD with the German Federal Foreign Office and the Berlin Senate
funding: The DAAD runs the programme with help from the German Federal Foreign Office and the Senate of Berlin, an arrangement in place since 1965 (Wikipedia).
The Ford Foundation created the programme in 1963 with an initial donation of three million US dollars (Wikipedia).
details.bottom_line: The daadgalerie belongs to the Berliner Künstlerprogramm, which the DAAD runs with the assistance of the German Federal Foreign Office and the Senate of Berlin (Wikipedia). The programme leaves Oranienstraße 161 on 30 September 2026.

name: Deutsche Oper Berlin
funding: The pages read did not state who funds the Deutsche Oper or give amounts for it. A Berlin parliament committee document lists the state grant to the Stiftung Oper in Berlin, Berlin's opera foundation, at EUR 174,357,000 for 2026.
watch: Aviel Cahn is named as Intendant on the opera's site, which also names Maxime Pascal, Michele Spotti and Titus Engel as its conductors.
records_note: The pages read gave no accounts.

overview: The Deutsche Oper Berlin is an opera house in Charlottenburg, Berlin; its site names Aviel Cahn as Intendant (opera website).
The pages read did not state its founding year or building history.

What is there: a team of three conductors (Maxime Pascal, Michele Spotti, Titus Engel), composer in residence Bára Gísladóttir and poet in residence Fiston Mwanza Mujila; singers are named within individual productions (opera website).
Archive: the pages read did not describe an archive.
details.funding_verdict: Deutsche Oper Berlin: public; the pages read did not name its funders
funding: Berlin parliament committee document (created 13 November 2025): Zuschuss an die Stiftung Oper in Berlin, EUR 174,357,000 for 2026 and EUR 180,798,000 for 2027. The pages read did not state which share goes to the Deutsche Oper.
No reporting found of private sponsors on the pages read.
details.bottom_line: The pages read name no funder or sum for the Deutsche Oper itself. Berlin's grant to its opera foundation is public, but the house's share was not found.

name: Deutsches Historisches Museum
funding: A federal public-law foundation runs the museum.
tier_note: No reason for the flag is recorded.
highlight: The Zeughaus has been closed for renovation since 2021, and the Exhibition Hall designed by I. M. Pei stays open.

overview: National history museum at Unter den Linden 2, 10117 Berlin, run by the Deutsches Historisches Museum Foundation (stated by the space).

Founded in 1987 by the Federal Republic of Germany and the Land of Berlin to mark Berlin's 750th anniversary. After reunification in 1990 it took over the buildings and collections of the GDR's Museum für Deutsche Geschichte (stated by the space). It first opened in the Reichstag building in former West Berlin (Wikipedia).

Prof. Dr. Raphael Gross, a Swiss historian, was appointed president by the Board of Trustees on 24 November 2016 and took office on 15 April 2017. The collection holds some 1,000,000 objects (stated by the space).

Buildings: the Zeughaus of 1695 and the adjacent exhibition hall designed by I. M. Pei, opened in 2003 (Wikipedia). The Zeughaus and the overview exhibition on German history are closed for construction (stated by the space). The Berliner Zeitung dates the closure to 2021.

The Pei building stays open with temporary exhibitions, daily from 10 am to 6 pm. The museum offers information in German Sign Language and Easy Language, a tactile orientation plan and barrier-free guided tours (stated by the space).
details.funding_verdict: Deutsches Historisches Museum: funded by the Federal Government Commissioner for Culture and the Media (stated by the space)
funding: The museum's site footer reads "Funded by the Federal Government Commissioner for Culture and the Media" (stated by the space).

Since 30 December 2008 the museum has been a public law foundation of the federal government (Wikipedia). Its Board of Trustees has five members from the Federal Government, the Bundestag and the Länder, and Dr. Konrad Schmidt-Werthern is chairman (stated by the space).

press.overall: Two pieces: a 2017 review of a 2016 exhibition and 2026 press coverage of the delayed Zeughaus renovation.

items.title: Jessica Aimufua, "Where Are You Going, White Man?" (10 April 2017), review of the exhibition "German Colonialism: Fragments Past and Present"
points: Calls the exhibition "an undeniably German and therefore Eurocentric perspective on colonial rule"; the Namibian and Tanzanian curators "were only called in" when the concept was largely complete.
The review calls the "Kolonfiguren" approach "dangerous" because it equates satirical exaggeration and racist stereotyping; the accompanying information "remains largely superficial".

The exhibition "displays too many objects in a confined space", around 500 exhibits on 1,000 square metres, and the installation on the Black Movement in Germany is "almost hidden in the far corner of the exhibition hall".

items.title: Kai Kleinwächter, "Sanierung außer Kontrolle: Zeughaus bleibt noch für Jahre zu" (23 January 2026)
points: The closure began in 2021 with damage to the air-conditioning system, when only a technical repair of the climate system was planned; the work now also covers IT and energy efficiency, a second visitor entrance and additional toilets.
Raphael Gross does not expect the Zeughaus to reopen before 2031, according to rbb24 as cited by the paper, and calls 2031 a positive scenario.
The paper reports renewed debate over costly construction projects and calls for interim solutions to show parts of the new permanent exhibition.

details.bottom_line: The money behind the museum is the German federal government, through the Commissioner for Culture and the Media, with the foundation overseen by a board of federal, Bundestag and Länder representatives. It was criticised for an exhibition's treatment of colonial history and the delayed Zeughaus renovation.
